title: Deep kernel
text: The mixed model compares individuals through their relatedness: either directly read from the genetic similarity (GBLUP, RR-BLUP), or learnt from neural network embeddings (deep kernel). This page puts these representations side by side and builds the deep kernel intuition step by step: from the genomic kinship and the ridge regression, through the neural network alone, to m2n2.

title: Deep kernel
text:
Materials and methods
The following representations are computed from the Arabidopsis thaliana 1001 Genomes data (Alonso-Blanco et al., 2016), packaged by meiosim. The genotypes are 10,000 SNPs randomly sampled among those of the RegMap panel (Horton et al., 2012). The accessions were collected in different countries, the country of origin of each accession defines its group, and its color in the figures. The phenotype is the days to flowering (DTF1) from the easyGWAS project (Grimm et al., 2017).
The neural network used in this example is ToyNN, a small network provided with m2n2 for didactic purposes.

title: Deep kernel
text:
Linear genomic model

Genomic kinship
The genomic kinship is classically computed as:
\[
K = \frac{W W^\top}{\sum_j 2p_j(1-p_j)},
\]
with \(W\) the centered markers and \(p_j\) the allele frequencies (VanRaden, 2008). It represents the genetic relatedness between individuals.








Figure 1: Genomic kinship \(K\), accessions sorted by country.



This structure can also be observed by a principal component analysis of the SNP matrix.








Figure 2: First three principal components of the genomic kinship \(K\), accessions colored by country.





Ridge regression
The ridge regression on the markers, \(y = \mathbf{1}\mu + Wa + r\) with \(W\) the centered allele incidence and \(a \sim N(0, \sigma^2_a I)\), is equivalent to the GBLUP on \(K\). The weighted alleles \(W \odot \hat a\) (with \(\odot\) the Hadamard product) decompose the prediction: their row sum is the predicted breeding value.








Figure 3: Principal components of the weighted alleles \(W \odot \hat a\) of the ridge regression.



Their principal components remain close to those of the kinship: the effects associated with the markers are estimated as infinitesimal, all small and of similar magnitude, so that they reweight the marker space almost uniformly, and the contrasts between individuals emerge from their sum.

title: Deep kernel
text:
Neural network
A network trained alone predicts \(\hat y = e^\top w + b\), with \(e\) the embeddings of its last layer.








Figure 4: Principal components of the embeddings \(e\) of the network trained alone.



Entirely built for the prediction, their space collapses to a single dimension, parallel to \(\hat y\). The same pattern is observed for \(e \odot w\), whose row sums are \(\hat y - b\).








Figure 5: Principal components of the weighted embeddings \(e \odot w\) of the network trained alone.

title: Deep kernel
section: Mixed model with a neural network
text:
Mixed model with a neural network
m2n2 is a (potentially) deep kernel (Wilson et al., 2016): the network builds an internal representation \(Z_G\), trained on \(y\) through the REML, but intermediate. The mixed model reads it as a covariance, \(\sigma^2_G Z_G Z_G^\top\), and sorts the general from the specific.

Embeddings








Figure 6: Principal components of the m2n2 embeddings \(Z_G\).



Though the 3D view cannot display it fully, the spherical normalization shows, and structures the embedding space.
As for the markers, a kinship is computed from the centered embeddings \(Z_c\):
\[
K_Z = \frac{Z_c Z_c^\top}{\sum_j \mathrm{var}(z_j)}.
\]
It is a proximity not in the genome, but in the learnt embeddings.








Figure 7: Embedding kinship \(K_Z\), accessions sorted by country.





General weighted embeddings
\(Z_G \odot \hat u_G\), whose row sums are the general part of the predicted value.








Figure 8: Principal components of the general weighted embeddings \(Z_G \odot \hat u_G\).



Just like the infinitesimal effects of the ridge regression barely alter the marker space, the general embedding effects is reminescent to the embedding space: both views are close.


Specific weighted embeddings
\(Z_G \odot \hat u_{S,k(i)}\), with \(k(i)\) the group of individual \(i\), whose row sums are the specific part of the predicted genetic value.








Figure 9: Principal components of the specific weighted embeddings \(Z_G \odot \hat u_{S,k(i)}\).



As opposed to the general part, the specific part differs strongly between groups, which are unequally shrunk. Poorly represented groups are shrunk to 0, while well represented ones receive their own specific embedding effects, accounted for and isolated from the general ones.


Observations
In this example, the embedding space is mostly shaped by the general part, which only slightly reweights it, but it already “prepares” the specific split: on the sphere, the large groups lie as adjacent sectors, like slices of a melon, that the specific effects pull apart along their own directions. The slices still overlap, especially on the first principal component of the embedding space: individuals from different groups are spread over a common range, across which the general effects can be estimated.
From a biological point of view, the specific effects represent a \(G \times G\) (genotype-by-genotype interaction, or epistasis) component, one \(G\) being the genetic specificity of the group, and the other \(G\) the whole genetic background. This component is difficult to interpret, and its subtraction aims at improving the model generalisability.

title: Deep kernel
text:
Beyond genomics
The embeddings do not need to come from markers: any input an encoder can turn into embeddings, such as text, images, sounds or more abstract concepts, defines a relatedness that the mixed model can read. For instance, embeddings of research paper titles, from a pretrained and frozen transformer, were used in a mixed model to explain their number of citations (Marchal et al., 2026).
m2n2 goes one step further: the encoder is trained jointly with the mixed model, on the same task.

Mixed modeling with neural networks, built on  .
The random design of a linear mixed model is the embedding of a neural network, trained jointly with the fixed effects and the variance components on the REML loss.

Installation
Install m2n2 with pip:
pip install m2n2

The model
m2n2 fits a linear mixed model built upon the neural network \(\nu\) of parameters \(\theta\):
\[
y = X\beta + Z_G u_G + Z_S u_S + r
\qquad
z_i \mapsto \nu(z_i, \theta) \in \mathbb{R}^d
\]

\(X\): fixed effects design matrix, provided from a patsy formula.
\(\beta\): fixed effects.
\(z_i\): features of individual \(i\) (e.g. SNPs).
\(Z_G = \nu(z, \theta)\): general design matrix, embedding of the features by the network of dimension \(n \times d\).
\(Z_S = \bigoplus_{k=1}^{q} \nu(z_{(k)}, \theta)\): specific design matrix of dimension \(n \times qd\) for the \(q\) groups.
\(u_G \sim N(0, \sigma^2_G I), u_G \in \mathbb{R}^d\): general embedding effects.
\(u_S \sim N(0, \sigma^2_S I), u_{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{qd}\): group-specific embedding effects (optional).
\(r \sim N(0, \sigma^2_R I)\): residual.

Example
from functools import partial
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from meiosim import Arabidopsis
from meiosim.Population import MISSING
from m2n2 import MixedModelNN

pop = Arabidopsis(n_SNPs=10_000, seed=42)
data = pop.phenotypes[["individual", "DTF1"]].merge(
    pop.metadata[["individual", "country"]], on="individual"
)

z = pop.genotypes.astype(np.float32)
z[z == MISSING] = np.nan
z = torch.tensor(np.where(np.isnan(z), np.nanmean(z, axis=0), z))

class Network(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, z):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("z", z)
        self.body = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
            nn.Linear(z.shape[1], 256), nn.BatchNorm1d(256), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.BatchNorm1d(128), nn.GELU(), nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(128, 64),
        )

    def forward(self, rows=None):
        return self.body(self.z if rows is None else self.z[rows])

torch.manual_seed(42)
network = Network(z) # /!\ z and data must be perfectly aligned

model = MixedModelNN.from_dataframe(
    data,
    response="DTF1",
    Z=network,
    specificity="country",
    optimizer=partial(
        torch.optim.AdamW,
        lr=1e-3,
        weight_decay=1e-1
    ),
    lr_beta=1e-2,
    lr_var=1e-2,
)

model.fit(
    n_epoch=1000,
    batch_size=256,
    validation=0.2,
    patience=50,
    verbose=False,
)


fig, (ax_loss, ax_score) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5))
ax_loss.plot(model.loss)
ax_loss.set_xlabel("epoch")
ax_loss.set_ylabel("REML -2logLik")
ax_score.plot(model.score)
ax_score.axvline(np.argmin(model.score), color="grey", linestyle="--")
ax_score.set_xlabel("epoch")
ax_score.set_ylabel("validation MSE")
plt.show()

model.plot()

model.varcomp()

title: Building models
text: m2n2 builds a model with MixedModelNN.from_dataframe(), from a pandas DataFrame and a PyTorch network.

title: Building models
text:
The from_dataframe constructor
model = MixedModelNN.from_dataframe(
    data        = data,
    response    = "DTF1",
    Z           = network,
    specificity = "country",
    fixed       = "1",
    optimizer   = partial(torch.optim.AdamW, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-1),
    lr_beta     = 1e-2,
    lr_var      = 1e-2,
)

model.fit()



Argument
Meaning




data
One row per individual.


response
One response column.


Z
The network \(\nu\), an nn.Module returning the embeddings (see the network).


specificity
Qualitative column defining the \(q\) groups of \(Z_S\). Defaults to None: no group-specific effect.


fixed
A patsy formula for \(X\). Defaults to the intercept "1".


optimizer
A torch.optim optimizer, LBFGS excepted, as a factory of the parameter groups. Defaults to partial(torch.optim.AdamW, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-1).


lr_beta
Learning rate of \(\beta\). Defaults to the optimizer’s.


lr_var
Learning rate of the variances. Defaults to the optimizer’s.

title: Building models
text:
The network
The network is user-defined, under the following contract:

Z() returns the \(n \times d\) embedding of every row of data, in the same order. Aligning the two is the user’s responsibility: only the number of rows is checked.
Z(rows), with rows a boolean mask over the rows of data, returns the embeddings of the selected rows only. Training feeds the labelled rows of each minibatch alone, so that batch statistics (e.g. BatchNorm) never see the others.
The model runs in the dtype and on the device of the output of Z().

The features \(z\) are typically stored in the network as a buffer:
class Network(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, z):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("z", z)
        self.body = nn.Sequential(...)

    def forward(self, rows=None):
        return self.body(self.z if rows is None else self.z[rows])
The embeddings are projected on the unit sphere before entering the mixed model (see Deep kernel). Dropout and BatchNorm belong to the network: m2n2 switches it to train() mode for the gradient steps, and to eval() mode for validation and prediction.

title: Building models
text:
Data layout and missing values

A row missing the response is left out of the fit, but still predicted.
A row missing a fixed covariate is left out of the fit.
specificity must be qualitative and complete: numeric codes are to be cast to str.

The random design \([Z_G \mid Z_S]\) has \(d(1 + q)\) columns, \(d\) without specificity.

title: Building models
text:
Initialization
The variances \(\sigma^2_G\), \(\sigma^2_S\) and \(\sigma^2_R\) are log-parameterized and initialized at the variance of the response. \(\beta\) is initialized by ordinary least squares on the labelled rows.
optimizer is called on four parameter groups:

title: Building models
text:
The fitted model
After .fit() (see Training models):



Accessor
Content




model.prediction
\(Z_G \hat u_G + Z_S \hat u_S\) for every row of data, missing responses included. Fixed effects excluded.


model.estimates
Fixed-effect estimates (BLUE) as a long table response · term · estimate · SE · t.


model.uhat_general
\(\hat u_G\), of shape (d,).


model.uhat_specific
\(\hat u_S\), of shape (q, d), one row per level of model.levels.


model.PEV
Prediction error variance of \([\hat u_G, \hat u_S]\).


model.residuals
Residuals of the labelled rows.


model.varcomp()
Raw and unit variances (see Deep kernel).


model.AIC
Akaike information criterion, post REML.


model.loss, model.score
Training curves (see Monitoring).


model.pca
PCA of the raw and weighted embeddings: coords, inertia, eigvec per embedding.


model.plot(plan=(0, 1))
Individual projections on the principal plan plan, colored by group.

title: Training models
text: m2n2 trains the network \(\nu\), the fixed effects \(\beta\) and the variances jointly, by minibatch gradient descent on the REML loss. The network is then frozen, and the mixed model is polished by pyreml.

title: Training models
text:
The fit method
model.fit(
    n_epoch    = 1000,
    batch_size = None,
    validation = 0.1,
    patience   = 50,
    verbose    = True,
)







Argument
Meaning




n_epoch
Maximum number of epochs. Defaults to 1000.


batch_size
Rows per minibatch. Defaults to None: full batch.


validation
Fraction of the labelled rows held out for early stopping. Defaults to None: no validation.


patience
Epochs without improvement of the validation score before stopping. Defaults to 50, None never stops.


verbose
Prints the loss and the score at each epoch.



The pipeline:

REML descent of \(\theta\), \(\beta\) and the variances, on minibatches (see Loss function).
Validation at each epoch, early stopping and restoration of the best state.
Polish: REML and HMME with the network frozen.

title: Training models
text:
Loss function
Once the random effects are integrated out, the model reads:
\[
y \sim N\big(X\beta,\ V\big),
\qquad
V = \sigma^2_G Z_G Z_G^\top + \sigma^2_S Z_S Z_S^\top + \sigma^2_R I,
\]
with \(Z_G = \nu(z, \theta)\). The network parameters \(\theta\) only enter \(V\): like \(\sigma^2_G\), \(\sigma^2_S\) and \(\sigma^2_R\), they are variance parameters, estimated jointly with \(\beta\) by restricted maximum of likelihood (REML):
\[
-2\ell_{\text{REML}} = \log\lvert V\rvert
+ r^\top V^{-1} r
+ \log\lvert X^\top V^{-1} X\rvert
+ (n - p) \log(2\pi),
\qquad
r = y - X\beta.
\]
\(u_G\) and \(u_S\) do not enter the loss: they are predicted afterwards by solving Henderson’s mixed model equations (HMME).

Minibatches
At each epoch, the labelled training rows are shuffled and split into minibatches of batch_size rows, the incomplete last batch dropped. As the embedding is computed row-wise, the covariance of a minibatch \(B\) is the submatrix \(V_B\) of \(V\), and \(y_B \sim N(X_B\beta, V_B)\) exactly: the loss of a minibatch is the REML of the corresponding sub-model. The random effects are iid, but the observations are not: they share \(u_G\), and \(V\) is not diagonal. The minibatch losses therefore do not add up to the full REML: minibatch descent is a stochastic approximation of it, which performs well empirically (Simchoni & Rosset, 2023).
The loss is computed by pyreml, on the SMW path when \(d(1+q) < n_B\), on \(V_B\) directly otherwise. The gradient flows by autograd through the variances, \(\beta\) and the network, and is applied by optimizer, AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) by default.
model.loss records the mean minibatch loss of each epoch. It scales with \(n_B\): curves are comparable at fixed batch_size only.

title: Training models
text:
Validation and early stopping
Trained on the marginal likelihood, a deep kernel can overfit more severely than a network trained alone (Ober et al., 2021). For this reason, an early stopping strategy is proposed my m2n2.
With validation set, a fraction of the labelled rows is held out once, at random. At each epoch, the network in eval() mode, the held-out rows \(v\) are predicted by their BLUP from the training rows \(t\):
\[
\hat y_v = X_v \beta + Z_v G Z_t^\top V_t^{-1} (y_t - X_t \beta),
\qquad
V_t = Z_t G Z_t^\top + \sigma^2_R I,
\]
with \(Z = [Z_G \mid Z_S]\) and \(G\) the diagonal of the variances. Their mean squared error is recorded in model.score.
The best state (network weights, \(\beta\), variances) is kept. Training stops after patience epochs without improvement, and the best state is restored. Without validation, training runs n_epoch epochs and the last state is kept.
Each validation solves a dense system in \(V_t\), of size \(n_t \times n_t\).
The held-out rows, the minibatches, the network initialization and the dropout masks all draw from the PyTorch generator: torch.manual_seed makes the training reproducible.

title: Training models
text:
Polish
The network is frozen in eval() mode and the embeddings computed once. The model is then a linear mixed model with a known random design, refitted by pyreml on every labelled row, held-out ones included:

REML re-estimates \(\beta\) and the variances, by L-BFGS with its adaptive convergence criterion;
HMME gives the BLUE of \(\beta\), the BLUP of \(u_G\) and \(u_S\), and their error variances.

Both run in the dtype of the network output.

text:
Monitoring







Accessor
Content




model.loss
Mean minibatch REML loss at each epoch.


model.score
Validation MSE at each epoch, empty without validation.


model.opti_REML.loss
REML loss at each iteration of the polish.


model.opti_REML.converged
Whether the polish met the convergence criterion.


model.opti_REML.duration
Wall-clock time of the polish, in seconds.




Training curves
Typical training behavior:



The validation MSE rises once the network overfits; the dashed line marks the restored epoch, from which the polish is run.
